\section*{S1. Render scalability}

The harness (\path{scripts/perf_benchmark.js --sweep}, documented in
\path{bench/render/README.md}) loads synthetic networks of 1,000 to 100,000
nodes with 1.5 or 5 edges per node into GLL in a fresh headless Chromium for
each run (viewport $1600\times900$, device pixel ratio 1) and measures load
time and frame rates during real wheel-zoom and mouse-drag input. Nodes are
placed in eight Gaussian clusters with 85\,\% of edges inside a cluster, and
the layout is precomputed, so no force layout is timed. Three styling
variants are tested: \emph{plain} (application defaults; labels are hidden
automatically above 1,000 nodes), \emph{heavy} (fill colour mapped from a
categorical property, size from a numeric property, labels forced on for
every node, curved edges with arrows, edge colour and width mapped from data)
and \emph{overlays} (\emph{heavy} plus animated flow on every edge, four
bubble groups of up to 500 members and the density heatmap). Headless
Chromium limits \texttt{requestAnimationFrame} to 60\,Hz, so 60 frames per
second (FPS) is the ceiling.

Table~\ref{tab:render} reports the medians of three runs on a workstation
(Intel Xeon w5-2465X, NVIDIA RTX A4000 16\,GB, Debian 13, Chromium 148, GLL
1.18.0 at commit \texttt{91eb61f}). The largest networks for which the
median zoom and pan rate both stayed at or above 30\,FPS were 50,000 nodes
(plain, both edge densities), 25,000 and 10,000 nodes (heavy, 1.5 and 5 edges
per node; in both series one smaller size fell below 30\,FPS while panning,
see the table note) and 5,000 and 1,000 nodes (overlays). On a laptop with an
integrated GPU (AMD Ryzen AI 9 HX 370 with Radeon 890M, Fedora 44, commit
\texttt{c931484}) the corresponding sizes were 50,000 and 25,000 (plain),
5,000 and 1,000 (heavy), and 1,000 and none (overlays).

\section*{S2. Assistant query generation}

Schema-constrained decoding guarantees that a generated query is well formed,
not that it is correct. The benchmark (\path{bench/assistant/}) therefore
compares the selection of each generated query with the selection of a
hand-written gold query. The gold set holds 52 questions on two networks, the
ADPKD model of this study (Supplementary datafile S1; 33 questions) and the
airport network template shipped with GLL (19 questions), in six tiers:
\emph{numeric} (a single numeric range; 9 questions), \emph{categorical} (a
single \texttt{IN} or \texttt{IS TRUE} condition; 9), \emph{two-clause} (two
conditions joined by \texttt{AND} or \texttt{OR}; 10), \emph{nested} (three or
more conditions, nesting or binary \texttt{NOT}; 8), \emph{paraphrase} (the
wording does not match the property name; 11) and \emph{impossible} (no
property can answer the question, so the correct answer is no query; 5).

For each question the harness imports the network with GLL's own Excel
import, builds the graph snapshot that the assistant panel sends, and calls
the application's query generator with its Ollama client (structured output
constrained to the network's properties, temperature 0, context window
16,384 tokens, including the generator's single repair pass). The first valid
suggested query is evaluated with GLL's query parser, as the panel's
\emph{Select} button does, and its node and edge IDs are compared with the
gold selection. A question counts as \emph{exact} when both ID sets are
identical; an impossible question counts as exact only when no query is
returned. Each question was run three times per model on a workstation with
an NVIDIA RTX A4000 (16\,GB) running Ollama
% CONFIRM(authors): the run metadata says Ollama 0.40.11, but mimo-v2.6
% requires >= 0.40.15. Check `ollama --version` on the workstation.
0.40.11; all models were 4-bit quantized (Q4\_K\_M). Latency is the
wall-clock time of the whole generation call, repair pass included; no
warm-up was run, so the slowest calls include loading the model.

\paragraph{Notes.}\sloppy
\texttt{mimo-v2.6} is the Ollama tag \texttt{mimo-v2.6:latest}
of MiMo-V2.6-Distill-Qwen-9B
(\url{https://huggingface.co/XiaomiMiMo/MiMo-V2.6-Distill-Qwen-9B}).
Within each run, \texttt{qwen3.5:9b} and \texttt{mimo-v2.6} returned identical
results in all three repeats; for \texttt{qwen3.5:4b} the outcome of one question varied.
An earlier \texttt{qwen3.5:9b} run on the same machine, while other jobs were
loading the GPU, scored 84.6\,\% exact because two questions changed outcome
(\path{2026-11-06T14-10-07-527Z.json}); temperature is 0 but no seed is set,
so the remaining variation comes from the server. Replies that Ollama
returned empty (\texttt{qwen3.5:4b}: 3, \texttt{mimo-v2.6}: 6 of 156) count as
no query. Most failures of \texttt{mimo-v2.6} on nested questions were no
query at all (12 of 21), whereas the Qwen models mostly returned a valid but
different selection.
